name: Base Attack to Sweep
summary: Aoki defense addresses a rotated foot and its hip connection; arm extraction or a sweep requires a separate, clearly established positional setup.
description: Base Attack to Sweep from Aoki Lock Control needs a defined reversal setup. Release the rotated foot safely before testing the opponent's posts and balance.
overview:
The endangered player has a turned-out foot enclosed by the opponent's upper body during a leg-entanglement exchange. An Aoki lock does not trap the arm in an omoplata. Do not rotate to turtle or bridge into a reversal while the foot remains fixed; these named destinations are not established by the reviewed foot-lock instruction.

A turned-out foot enclosed beside the armpit is a rotational threat, not simply a straight ankle-lock grip. Prevent the foot enclosure and recover leg position while the opponent still lacks a secure connection. Do not spin the torso while the foot remains fixed.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Rob Biernacki — the Aoki lock](https://www.grapplearts.com/the-step-by-step-aoki-lock/); [IBJJF — current rule resources](https://ibjjf.com/books-videos).

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): What makes a bridge risky in the initial Aoki capture?
flashcards.answer: Do not bridge into a reversal while a turned foot and hip remain controlled by the Aoki enclosure.
flashcards.answer_line: Turned foot against a restrained hip

plausible: Heel turns freely in a straight grip
Hip and sole rise without restraint
trap: Only calf pressure, no heel rotation

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): What is the early hand-fighting target?
flashcards.answer: Prevent the foot enclosure and recover leg position while the opponent still lacks a secure connection.
flashcards.answer_line: Arms closing around your turned foot

plausible: The palm on your uncaptured knee
The hip frame as their hands join

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): Which body relationship must remain aligned?
flashcards.answer: Do not spin the torso while the foot remains fixed.
flashcards.answer_line: Knee and foot as your torso moves

plausible: Hips and shoulders, heel still fixed
Knee inward, foot staying outward
trap: Foot stays fixed as pelvis circles

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): Before trying a reversal, what must be dismantled?
flashcards.answer: Reversal mechanics come later; first remove the hand enclosure and leg/hip restraint without twisting.

plausible: Just hip frame, heel still enclosed
Just clasp, instep still clamped
trap: Free leg's hook, trapped leg held

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): Why is lack of pain insufficient permission to sweep?
flashcards.answer: Tap early to a secure rotational lock rather than treating the absence of pain as safety.
flashcards.answer_line: Rotation may load before pain warns

plausible: Knee stays unloaded during hip turns
Relaxed calf means free ankle motion
trap: No pain permits a trial bridge

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): After release, which movement rebuilds a guard barrier?
flashcards.answer: After opening the foot and hip controls, recover the knee and a facing frame before considering a new attack.
flashcards.answer_line: Freed knee in behind a torso frame

plausible: Leave knee back, reach a far sleeve
Turn knees away, reach over them
trap: Shift hips back, leave knee outside

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): Why must a mobile hip not be used to turn a trapped heel?
flashcards.answer: Hip freedom does not establish foot freedom. Release the foot enclosure and leg restraint before any separately established reversal so the knee can follow the foot.
flashcards.answer_line: Knee twists above the fixed foot

plausible: Hip motion opens the arm clamp first
Ankle takes the turn, knee unloaded
trap: Leg clamp makes foot follow pelvis

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): What does release of Aoki still leave unestablished?
flashcards.answer: A released foot does not supply a sweep. A new base-breaking setup must be established separately.

plausible: Just a post, balance already broken
Just landing, posts already held
trap: Just hip lift, freed foot is a lever

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): Your hips can move but the heel stays caught. What now?
flashcards.answer: Hip mobility alone does not free a captured heel; do not use it to force a reversal.
flashcards.answer_line: Stop turning; get the foot released

plausible: Bridge on while turning shoulders
Pull knee out before arm clamp opens
trap: Free your leg hook and keep turning

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (escaping player): What should a recognition drill identify first?
flashcards.answer: Identify the starting configuration and rehearse the first connection without finishing pressure. A turned-out foot enclosed beside the armpit is a rotational threat, not simply a straight ankle-lock grip.
flashcards.answer_line: The outward foot held by the armpit

plausible: A straight foot loose on the forearm
A cupped heel with instep outside
trap: A calf on forearm, heel below it

defender.overview:

Recognize the foot orientation without twisting it into position against resistance. Hold the instep and heel region securely beside the upper body rather than relying on calf compression. Use the entanglement or foot-on-hip frame to manage distance before considering a finish.

Stop the drill at a secure capture; the control can become a damaging rotation with very little movement. Keep track of your own exposed feet while concentrating on the captured foot. Open the arm enclosure and remove leg pressure immediately on a tap, sudden movement, or pain.

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (foot-locker): What lower-limb cue makes Aoki capture available?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the foot orientation without twisting it into position against resistance.
flashcards.answer_line: An outward foot within arm reach

plausible: An inward foot beside your upper arm
A straight ankle, instep outside arm
trap: Outward foot too far, heel hidden

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (foot-locker): What distinguishes your grip from calf compression?
flashcards.answer: Hold the instep and heel region securely beside the upper body rather than relying on calf compression.
flashcards.answer_line: Instep and heel enclosed by armpit

plausible: Calf folded over shin at knee crease
Calf squeeze with the instep outside

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (foot-locker): What stops the opponent freely following the captured foot?
flashcards.answer: Use the entanglement or foot-on-hip frame to manage distance before considering a finish.
flashcards.answer_line: A leg connection controlling the hip

plausible: A loose hand on the uncaptured knee
Hands on toes, legs disengaged
trap: Shin on thigh with no hip block

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (foot-locker): Why avoid adding extension as the opponent attempts to bridge?
flashcards.answer: Stop the drill at a secure capture; the control can become a damaging rotation with very little movement.
flashcards.answer_line: Bridging may load the fixed foot

plausible: Bridge shortens lever, extend more
Extension unloads the rising knee
trap: Tighter grip keeps the drill aligned

flashcards.question: Base Attack to Sweep (foot-locker): What counter threatens your outward hip-posting foot?
flashcards.answer: Keep track of your own exposed feet while concentrating on the captured foot.

plausible: An enclosure loading Achilles only
A heel-only grip, instep outside
trap: An ankle grip allowing free rotation
